analysis.one_liner: Restores FTC authority to regulate junk food marketing aimed at children.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in a House subcommittee with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1980, a legal rider has barred the Federal Trade Commission from writing rules that restrict advertising to children. This bill would repeal that rider, letting the FTC limit marketing of foods and drinks to children under 18 when evidence shows those products harm their health. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it died without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and families gain if the bill passes: it would let the FTC restrict junk food ads aimed at kids, a step the Institute of Medicine recommended amid rising childhood obesity and type 2 diabetes. Parents benefit from less marketing pressure on young children who, as the bill's findings note, cannot understand advertising's persuasive intent.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the FTC Act provision that denies the FTC authority to write rules on children's advertising, restoring its power to act [S2][S3].
Would let the FTC restrict marketing of foods and beverages to children under 18 when evidence shows consumption is harmful to children's health [S3].
Cites findings that childhood obesity has tripled, over 12 million children and adolescents are overweight, and type 2 diabetes has become widespread in children [S3].

Notes the Institute of Medicine found food products targeted at children grew from 52 new introductions in 1994 to nearly 500 in 2005, with $15 billion spent on junk food marketing in 2005, and recommended giving the FTC this authority [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Food and beverage makers and the advertising industry would bear the cost: restrictions on marketing to children could shrink sales of products that depend heavily on ads aimed at young viewers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Food makers and the ad industry

drawbacks.text: A valid objection is that marketing restrictions are a blunt tool: the FTC could sweep in a wide range of foods, and the bill lets it regulate based on its own determinations about which products harm children's health, which could raise overreach and free-speech concerns [S3].

The bill's own findings acknowledge the FTC proposed a ban on TV ads directed at children under 8 in the late 1970s, and Congress chose not to grant that authority then, an objection Congress would likely raise again [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health case for letting the FTC regulate ads to children is substantial, given the bill's findings on childhood obesity and the Institute of Medicine's recommendation. The cost falls on food and advertising companies, and the main risk is regulatory overreach in defining which foods are covered. The bill was so narrow — one sentence repealing one subsection — that it made no attempt to address those design questions.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection subcommittee until the Congress ended, with no hearing or vote.

narrative.text: Delegate Eleanor Holmes Norton introduced the bill on June 29, 2006 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S5].
On July 17, 2006, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection, where it stayed for the rest of the 109th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food and beverage marketers and the advertising industry, which keep unrestricted freedom to advertise foods to children, including to young children who cannot recognize advertising as persuasion.

for.name: Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill died in committee with no cosponsors, so no record of support or opposition exists.

industries.note: The bill would let the FTC restrict marketing of foods and drinks to children under 18, threatening the sales of products sold heavily through child-directed advertising. Its failure keeps that marketing channel unrestricted.

Roughly $15 billion a year was spent on junk food marketing in 2005 by the bill's own findings; restoring FTC rulemaking authority over children's ads would directly limit this business. The bill's death preserves it.
